script:
This robot learned to walk like a human without taking a single real step.
This is Figure 02, and its entire walk was learned inside a physics simulator.
Think of it like a video game with real-world physics.
Inside it, thousands of virtual copies of this robot practice at the same time.
It's trial and error, and they're rewarded for moving more like a person.
Heel strikes, toe-offs, even the arm swing.
And the crazy part is the speed.
They simulate years of walking data in just a few hours.
On a real robot, that's slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous.
But here's the hard part.
A simulation is only an approximation of the real world.
Real motors lag, floors get slippery, and no two robots are exactly alike.
So Figure gives every virtual robot slightly different physics, then trips and shoves them constantly.
That way, the real world just feels like one more level of the game.
And it worked.
These are ten real robots running the exact same AI with zero tweaks.
It sounds crazy now, but in a few years, most robots will learn their skills before the real machine even switches on.

sources.supports: Figure 02's walking controller was trained fully in a physics simulator with reinforcement learning (trial and error with rewards); thousands of virtual Figure 02 robots are simulated in parallel, each with unique physical parameters; years of data simulated in a few hours; rewarded for mimicking human walking (heel strikes, toe-offs, arm swing); exposed to trips, slips and shoves; a simulated robot is only an approximation; domain randomization bridges the sim-to-real gap; the policy transfers zero-shot with no extra tuning and copes with robot-to-robot variation and changes in surface friction; 10 Figure 02 robots run the same neural network with no tweaks

Training on real hardware is slow, expensive and sometimes dangerous; real actuators have delay and respond less faithfully than simulated ones; with domain randomization, reality becomes just another sample of the variations the robot trained on; simulation-trained policies underpin much of legged locomotion

Independent confirmation that thousands of virtual humanoids walked simultaneously in simulation, were rewarded for arm swings, heel strikes and toe-offs, were tripped and shoved, and that the model was then applied to a physical Figure robot
